content.title: 2×2 Determinants and Matrix Equations
content.overview: This lesson covers the calculation of determinants for 2×2 matrices and the use of the matrix inverse to solve linear systems in the form Ax = b.
learning_objectives: Calculate the determinant of a 2×2 matrix.
Identify when a 2×2 matrix is invertible based on its determinant.
Construct the inverse of a 2×2 matrix using the shortcut method.
Solve matrix equations of the form Ax = b using the inverse matrix.

sections.title: The 2×2 Determinant
sections.content: For any 2×2 matrix A with entries [[a, b], [c, d]], the determinant (denoted as det(A) or |A|) is a scalar value calculated using the formula: det(A) = ad - bc. This value is critical because it determines if the matrix has an inverse. If det(A) = 0, the matrix is 'singular' and has no inverse. If det(A) ≠ 0, the matrix is 'invertible' or 'non-singular'.

sections.title: The 2×2 Inverse Shortcut
sections.content: To find the inverse of a 2×2 matrix A = [[a, b], [c, d]], follow three specific steps: 1. Calculate the determinant (ad - bc). 2. Create a new matrix by swapping the main diagonal elements (a and d) and changing the signs of the off-diagonal elements (b and c). This results in [[d, -b], [-c, a]]. 3. Multiply this new matrix by the scalar 1/det(A). The full formula is A⁻¹ = (1 / (ad - bc)) * [[d, -b], [-c, a]].

sections.title: Solving Matrix Equations
sections.content:
A system of linear equations can be written as Ax = b, where A is the coefficient matrix, x is the variable vector, and b is the constant vector. To solve for x, multiply both sides by the inverse: x = A⁻¹b. Note that matrix multiplication is not commutative; you must multiply the inverse by the constant vector in that specific order (A⁻¹ on the left).

![A flow chart showing the steps: Calculate Determinant, Check if Non-Zero, Construct Inverse Matrix, Multiply Inverse by Vector b.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/a4eebef5-8500-4cff-9d81-66ee857b9cd2-1786505599764-945.webp)

worked_examples.question: Solve for x in the equation Ax = b where A = [[2, 3], [1, 4]] and b = [5, 6].
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Find the determinant. det(A) = (2 * 4) - (3 * 1) = 8 - 3 = 5. Step 2: Construct the inverse matrix. Swap 2 and 4, and negate 3 and 1 to get [[4, -3], [-1, 2]]. Multiply by 1/det: A⁻¹ = 1/5 * [[4, -3], [-1, 2]]. Step 3: Multiply A⁻¹ by b. x = 1/5 * [[4, -3], [-1, 2]] * [5, 6]. Perform the multiplication: [ (4*5 + -3*6), (-1*5 + 2*6) ] = [ (20 - 18), (-5 + 12) ] = [2, 7]. Step 4: Apply the scalar: x = [2/5, 7/5].

common_mistakes: Subtracting in the wrong order when calculating the determinant (doing bc - ad instead of ad - bc).
Forgetting to negate the off-diagonal elements when forming the inverse.
Swapping the off-diagonal elements instead of the main diagonal elements.
Attempting to find an inverse when the determinant is zero.
exam_tips: If a question asks if a system has 'no solution' or 'infinitely many solutions,' check if the determinant of the coefficient matrix is zero.
Always perform a quick check by multiplying the first row of A by your solution vector x to see if it equals the first element of b.
content.recap: To solve Ax = b for a 2×2 matrix, calculate the determinant (ad-bc), construct the inverse by swapping the main diagonal and negating the off-diagonal, scale by 1/det, and multiply by vector b.

knowledge_claims.content: The determinant of a 2×2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] is calculated as ad - bc.
A 2×2 matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is not equal to zero.
A matrix with a determinant of zero is called a singular matrix and does not have an inverse.
To begin forming the 2×2 inverse, the elements on the main diagonal (top-left and bottom-right) must be swapped.
To form the 2×2 inverse, the signs of the off-diagonal elements (top-right and bottom-left) must be negated, but their positions remain the same.
The full formula for the inverse of matrix A is A⁻¹ = (1/det(A)) * [[d, -b], [-c, a]].
To solve the matrix equation Ax = b, you multiply the inverse matrix A⁻¹ by the constant vector b.
A common error is swapping the off-diagonal elements instead of simply negating their signs.
The validity of a solution x can be verified by checking if the product of the original matrix A and the solution x equals the constant vector b.
If the determinant of the coefficient matrix in a system of equations is zero, the system does not have a unique solution.
In the equation x = A⁻¹b, the inverse matrix must be placed to the left of the constant vector because matrix multiplication is not commutative.
The main diagonal of a 2×2 matrix consists of the elements 'a' (row 1, col 1) and 'd' (row 2, col 2).

videoLesson.description: Recognize when determinant ad−bc and entries make a 2×2 system invertible. Swap diagonals, negate off-diagonals, divide by ad−bc, and multiply by the constant vector to get x.
